sections.html:
Boone County sits northwest of Indianapolis, with Lebanon as the county seat. It is really two housing markets under one tax office. The southeast corner is suburban Zionsville, the largest town. The rest is Lebanon, smaller towns and farm country. The 2020 census counted 70,812 people, up 25.0% from 56,640 in 2010, and four separate school corporations serve the county.

Big projects change how owners think about timing. The LEAP Research and Innovation District covers more than 9,000 acres set aside for technology and manufacturing, and an Eli Lilly facility is planned there. Some owners expect strong demand and wait. Others, especially heirs, landlords and owners with deferred repairs, would rather sell now and skip the preparation. Both groups owe the same tax bill until closing.

Boone County property tax is paid to the county treasurer in two equal installments, due May 10 and November 10 under Indiana law. When May 10 falls on a weekend, the state calendar moves that date to the next business day.

The treasurer's office is on the second floor of the county courthouse in downtown Lebanon, open Monday through Friday from 8 a.m. to 4 p.m., and closed on legal holidays and Election Day. The phone is 765-482-2880.

  • In person: cash, personal checks, cashier checks, certified checks and money orders. Cards are accepted only online.
  • By mail: payable to Boone County Treasurer, 209 Courthouse Square, Lebanon, IN 46052. The envelope must carry a post office postmark by the due date, and a postage meter date does not count.
  • Online and phone: through the county's payment portal or 1-877-886-1892. Cards cost 2.95% with a $1.95 minimum. An ACH payment has a flat $0.95 fee.

Avoid paying by bank bill pay check, because those envelopes usually do not receive a post office postmark. If you are selling, pay the bill directly or give the title company a copy of it.

sections.h2: How to appeal in Boone County
sections.html:
You start an appeal by filing Form 130 with the Assessor's Office. Each spring the county mails assessment notices (Form 11) with the appeal deadline, which is June 15, printed at the top of the notice.

Before appealing, check your property record card. If it lists the wrong square footage, bathroom count, outbuildings or basement, the county offers a separate correction of error. Filing is allowed by email to assessmentappeal@co.boone.in.us, by mail or in person, and you should attach evidence. Someone other than the owner or a family member needs a signed power of attorney.

  1. The Assessor reviews your appeal after the deadline and contacts you for a preliminary hearing.
  2. If you cannot agree, the Property Tax Assessment Board of Appeals (PTABOA) hears the case, usually on a Wednesday, with notice by mail.
  3. You get a Form 115 with the board's decision.
  4. If you disagree, file Form 131 with the Indiana Board of Tax Review and send the Assessor a copy.
  5. After that decision you can seek review in the Indiana Tax Court.

An appeal can leave your value higher, lower or unchanged. The PTABOA hearing must occur within 180 days of filing, with at least 30 days of notice. See the Boone County Assessor appeal page for current forms.

sections.h2: Taxes and deductions when a house sells
sections.html:
Indiana requires a sales disclosure form signed by the buyer and seller before the deed is filed with the county auditor. The county assessor reviews it first, and each parcel needs its own form, with a single exception for contiguous parcels inside one taxing district.

Taxes are billed in arrears, so a spring or fall installment can fall due around your closing date. Title companies normally split the bill between buyer and seller by closing date, which you should confirm with your closing agent.

The homestead deduction also changes hands. The standard deduction has been 60% of assessed value, up to $48,000, and a new owner who buys after the assessment date can qualify by filing the statement or a sales disclosure form with the assessor by December 31 of the purchase year. The rule was amended effective January 1, 2025, so check with the Auditor for the current figure.

A late payment adds a penalty under Indiana law. Paying within 30 days of the due date adds 5% of the delinquent tax if there is no earlier delinquency on the parcel. In every other case the penalty is 10%.

Later installments can bring additional 10% penalties, and the penalties apply to the principal owed. Payments go first to the tax and then to the penalty. Past that point the parcel can be offered at a county tax sale, and Indiana owners generally have one year to redeem. Call the Boone County Treasurer for the timing on your parcel.

A house with a delinquent bill can still be sold. The unpaid tax and penalty are settled from the proceeds at closing, which is one reason sellers with several years of back tax often prefer a direct cash sale over listing.

Most Boone County sellers face one of a few situations: a house that needs work, an inherited property, a tenant, or a timing problem. A short prep list helps in each case.

  • Check your Form 11 value against what you would accept in a sale.
  • Pull the property record card and fix any errors before they affect a buyer's review.
  • Keep the latest tax bill, mortgage payoff and any estate papers ready.
  • Ask the treasurer for the current balance before scheduling a closing.

If you want to skip repairs, showings and appraisal delays, a cash offer for a Boone County house can close on your timeline, with tax proration handled at the title company. The county's southeast corner around Zionsville and the Lebanon area can feel like different markets, so ask for comparable sales close to your own address. Whichever route you take, plan the order of events: confirm the balance, sign the sales disclosure form, then let the title company file the deed with the auditor.

If you are close to the deadlines, a few details are worth knowing. A mailed check is on time only with a post office postmark, so a closing near a due date is better handled by paying online or in person. If the house is rented, the tenant does not change the bill, and the same installments apply. For an inherited house, bring the estate papers to the closing agent early so the payoff figure and the names on the deed match.

faqs.q: When are Boone County property taxes due?
faqs.a: In two equal installments on May 10 and November 10 under Indiana law. When May 10 lands on a weekend, the state calendar moves it. Mailed payments must be postmarked by the due date.

faqs.q: Where do I pay Boone County property tax in person?
faqs.a: At the treasurer's office on the second floor of the courthouse in downtown Lebanon, Monday through Friday, 8 a.m. to 4 p.m., except legal holidays and Election Day. Cash, checks, cashier checks and money orders are accepted in person, and cards are online only.

faqs.q: What is the deadline to appeal a Boone County assessment?
faqs.a: June 15, printed on your Form 11 each spring. File Form 130 with the Boone County Assessor, by email, mail or in person.

faqs.q: How much is the late penalty on Indiana property tax?
faqs.a: The penalty is 5% of the delinquent amount if you pay within 30 days of the due date and have no earlier delinquency on the parcel. Otherwise it is 10%. Additional 10% penalties can attach to later installments.

faqs.q: Can I sell a Boone County house with unpaid property tax?
faqs.a: Yes. The balance, plus any penalty, is paid from your proceeds at closing. Ask the treasurer for an exact payoff before the closing date.
